notes:
Here are my verse-by-verse notes on Genesis 13, compiled from the sources I was able to access.

---

## Genesis 13 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### v. 1 — *"So Abram went up out of Egypt into the Negev—he and his wife and all his possessions—and Lot was with him."*

- **The geography:** "Went up" reflects Egypt being low-lying and Canaan being higher. "The Negev" (or "the South") is the dry southern region of Canaan, virtually a proper name for that territory. (Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/13.htm; Ellicott: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/13.htm)
- **A special mercy:** The Pulpit Commentary notes it was a special mercy that Abram and Sarai returned at all, considering the sin they had committed in Egypt and the peril they had been in. (Pulpit: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-13.html)
- **Wasted time:** David Guzik (Enduring Word) observes that Abram returned to the same place he started. His time in Egypt was essentially wasted — God could have provided in Canaan even during famine. Though God brought good out of it, disobedience had a real cost. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-13/)
- **Lot's inclusion:** Lot is reintroduced into the narrative, having been absent from the Egypt episode. Gill notes that Lot clearly went down with Abram to Egypt and likely received favour there because of his relation to Abram and Sarai. (Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/13.htm)
- **"He went on his journeys":** Ellicott renders this "according to his stations," noting that the Vulgate reasonably translates it as "by the same route by which he had come." (Ellicott: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/13.htm)

### v. 2 — *"And Abram had become extremely wealthy in livestock and silver and gold."*

- **The Hebrew "very rich":** The word literally means "very heavy" — Abram was loaded or weighed down with wealth. (Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/13.htm; Pulpit: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-13.html)
- **Cattle (mikneh):** From a root meaning "to acquire by purchase." The Pulpit Commentary notes this term may apply to slaves as well as livestock, since slaves were considered chattel. (Pulpit: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-13.html)
- **Silver and gold:** Mentioned for the first time in Scripture, implying Egyptian acquaintance with mining and refining precious metals. Ellicott observes that gold was plentiful in Egypt at that time but silver was rare; Abram probably brought his silver from Mesopotamia. Silver and gold is listed after livestock, suggesting livestock was the primary form of wealth. (Ellicott: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/13.htm; Pulpit: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-13.html)
- **Source of wealth:** Gill notes that Abram's riches were greatly increased by gifts from Pharaoh during his stay in Egypt. (Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/13.htm)

### v. 3 — *"From the Negev he journeyed from place to place toward Bethel, until he came to the place between Bethel and Ai where his tent had formerly been pitched,"*

- **Retracing steps:** Abram journeyed by stages, retracing the same general route he had taken when first entering Canaan. Gill records the Jewish tradition (Jarchi) that Abram had "learned the way of the earth, that a man should not change his host." (Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/13.htm)
- **Bethel and Ai:** This was the location between Bethel and Ai (later called Mount Ephraim), about four miles north of Jerusalem. This is where Abram had pitched his tent on his first arrival in the land (Genesis 12:8). (Gill; Ellicott: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/13.htm)
- **Spiritual significance:** The Preacher's Complete Homiletical Commentary emphasizes that Abram returned to the scenes where God was first felt and known: "The believer, when his soul has been injured by the world, derives comfort and encouragement from the past — from revisiting the scenes where God was first felt and known." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/genesis-13.html)
- **Guzik:** Though Abram returned with great riches from Egypt, he came back to the same place as before — right back where he started. The Egypt sojourn was essentially wasted time. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-13/)

### v. 4 — *"to the site where he had built the altar. And there Abram called on the name of the LORD."*

- **The altar likely gone:** Gill speculates the altar was no longer standing — it may have fallen (being made of earth), been destroyed by Canaanites, or been pulled down by Abram himself before his departure to prevent idolatrous misuse. He came "to the place" of the altar, not to the altar itself. (Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/13.htm)
- **Calling on the name of the LORD:** Gill says this means Abram prayed and gave thanks for preservation in Egypt, for provision during the famine, for increase of wealth, and for protection during the journey. (Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/13.htm)
- **Not the first altar:** Ellicott clarifies that "at the first" means this was the altar Abram built on his first arrival at that spot. His very first altar in Canaan was at Shechem (Genesis 12:7). (Ellicott: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/13.htm)
- **Fresh consecration:** The Preacher's Complete Homiletical Commentary says this implies "a fresh consecration of himself… There is no new way of restoration. We must come back to Him who first gave us our faith and made reconciliation." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/genesis-13.html)
- **Worship as a public witness:** The Pulpit Commentary, citing Calvin and Luther, says that "calling on the name of the LORD" means Abram both professed the true worship of God publicly and taught his family and Canaanite neighbours the true religion. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-13.html)
- **Guzik:** Abram did what he should: instead of agonising over past sin, he lived with the tent as a pilgrim and the altar as a worshipper. God wants believers to walk in their "first love" and "first works" (Revelation 2:4-5). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-13/)

### v. 5 — *"Now Lot, who was traveling with Abram, also had flocks and herds and tents."*

- **Shared prosperity:** Lot shared in the blessing that came through Abram. The Pulpit Commentary says "the uncle's prosperity overflowed upon the nephew." Ellicott notes Lot "too, had possibly received presents in Egypt." (Pulpit: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-13.html; Ellicott: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/13.htm)
- **"Tents":** This indicates Lot had numerous followers and, like Abram, was chief of a powerful clan. Rosenmüller includes domestics and servants within the reference to "tents." (Ellicott; Pulpit)
- **Guzik:** God had commanded Abram to leave his family behind (Genesis 12:1), but Abram brought Lot. This trouble was the result of that incomplete obedience. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-13/)

### v. 6 — *"But the land was unable to support both of them while they stayed together, for they had so many possessions that they were unable to coexist."*

- **The land could not bear them:** The Pulpit Commentary notes this was partly due to scarce pasturage (the land possibly still recovering from the drought that drove them to Egypt) and partly due to their increasing wealth. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-13.html)
- **Long-standing problem:** Ellicott observes that the double statement ("the land was not able to bear them" and "they could not dwell together") implies the difficulty had long been felt before it led to open rupture. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/13.htm)
- **The irony of wealth:** Gill notes an irony: "what one would think would make them more comfortable together, is the cause and occasion of their separation." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/13.htm)
- **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary:** This was also due to the ravages of the drought from which the land was not fully recovered. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/genesis-13.html)

### v. 7 — *"And there was discord between the herdsmen of Abram and the herdsmen of Lot. At that time the Canaanites and the Perizzites were also living in the land."*

- **Source of strife:** The Pulpit Commentary says the strife originated in the scarcity of pasture and was about possession of the best wells and most fertile grounds. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-13.html)
- **The Canaanites and Perizzites:** Ellicott identifies the Perizzites as probably the earlier, pre-Hamite inhabitants of the country — a pastoral people without towns who maintained themselves in the open country. The term likely means "lowlander." The presence of these peoples explains why finding sufficient pasture was so difficult; the land was already occupied. (Ellicott: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/13.htm)
- **A witness before unbelievers:** Guzik stresses that when the Canaanites and Perizzites saw the herdsmen fighting, they would think, "See, they're just like we are. They say they worship another God… but I see they argue just as we often do." Gill similarly notes the danger: the neighbouring peoples might take advantage of their quarrels and fall upon them both. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-13/; Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/13.htm)
- **Barnhouse quoted by Guzik:** "Many people will never listen to what any believer says because of what some believers are." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-13/)
- **Spiritual attack:** Guzik also observes that this conflict came *after* Abram did the right thing — when believers get right with God, they may expect attack from the enemy. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-13/)

### v. 8 — *"So Abram said to Lot, 'Please let there be no contention between you and me, or between your herdsmen and my herdsmen. After all, we are brothers.'"*

- **Abram's initiative:** Though senior in years, superior in substance, and higher in relationship, Abram made the first proposal for peace. Gill: "he was a wise and good man." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/13.htm)
- **Lot's attitude:** Ellicott detects that Lot was beginning to take part with his herdsmen and regard himself as injured. Abram perceived that "Lot's face was not towards him as usual" (Pulpit) and moved to avert collision. (Ellicott: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/13.htm; Pulpit: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-13.html)
- **"We be brethren":** Literally "men, brethren we be" (Gill). The Pulpit Commentary expands: they were kinsmen by nature, by relationship, and by faith (cf. 2 Peter 2:7). This threefold bond obliged them to seek peace. (Gill; Pulpit)
- **Guzik:** Abram did not yield out of weakness but out of love and trust in God. A few acres of grazing land didn't seem worth fighting for to a man living with an eternal perspective. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-13/)
- **F.B. Meyer:** "Blessed are the peacemakers! Wherever the interests of peace can be conserved through the sacrifice of your own interests, be prepared to forfeit the advantage, but stand like a rock when God's truth is in balance." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/fbm/genesis-13.html)

### v. 9 — *"Is not the whole land before you? Now separate yourself from me. If you go to the left, I will go to the right; if you go to the right, I will go to the left.'"*

- **Extraordinary generosity:** Since the land had been promised to Abram (not Lot), and Abram was the elder, it was remarkable magnanimity to give Lot first choice. The Pulpit Commentary calls this a "sublime act of self-renunciation." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-13.html; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-13/)
- **Left and right explained:** Standing facing east (the ancient Hebrew orientation), the left hand pointed north and the right hand south. The Targums render it: "if thou wilt go to the north, I will go to the south." (Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/13.htm)
- **Constable's note (from search excerpt):** Abram was suggesting they partition the Promised Land. Since Hebrews were east-oriented, "left" referred to northern Canaan (around Shechem down to Bethel/Ai) and "right" to southern Canaan (Hebron and the Negev). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-13.html)
- **Trust in God:** Guzik emphasises that right or left, Abram knew he could trust God. In Egypt he had tried to take his fate into his own hands; now he was wiser and willing to let God look out for his interests. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-13/)
- **Henry's Concise Commentary:** "Those are best prepared for the visits of Divine grace, whose spirits are calm, and not ruffled with passion. God will abundantly make up in spiritual peace, what we lose for preserving neighbourly peace." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhn/genesis-13.html)

### v. 10 — *"And Lot looked out and saw that the whole plain of the Jordan, all the way to Zoar, was well watered like the garden of the LORD, like the land of Egypt. (This was before the LORD destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah.)"*

- **"Lifted up his eyes":** The Pulpit Commentary notes the Hebrew conveys "a look of eager, lustful greed" (cf. Genesis 3:6) — quite different from Abram's later looking in v.14. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-13.html)
- **The "plain" (Ciccar):** Literally "the circle" or surrounding region. Ellicott describes it as the Jordan valley (the Ghor), a deep geological depression, much of it below sea level. At that time the Jordan poured down far more water than today and the region was extraordinarily fertile. (Ellicott: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/13.htm)
- **"Like the garden of the LORD":** A reference to Eden, with its four rivers. The Pulpit Commentary and Gill both note this comparison — the Jordan plain reminded Lot of paradise itself. (Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/13.htm)
- **"Like the land of Egypt":** Lot had just seen Egypt's well-watered fertility. The Pulpit Commentary notes the Jordan plain, like Egypt, was irrigated — Egypt by the Nile and its canals, the Jordan plain by the river and its tributaries. (Pulpit: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-13.html)
- **"As thou comest unto Zoar":** Ellicott argues the Syriac preserves the correct reading here — not Zoar but *Zoan* (Tanis in Egypt), through whose fertile plain Lot had recently travelled with Abram. "As thou comest unto Zoar" makes little geographical sense on the route described. (Ellicott: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/13.htm)
- **The parenthetical note ("before the LORD destroyed…"):** This is a Mosaic editorial comment inserted to explain why the region described no longer looked like paradise at the time the narrative was written.

### v. 11 — *"So Lot chose the whole plain of the Jordan for himself and set out toward the east. And Abram and Lot parted company."*

- **Greedy acceptance:** Ellicott remarks that Lot, instead of feeling that deference to his uncle's age and rank required him to yield the preference back to Abram, "greedily accepts the offer." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/13.htm)
- **Journeyed east:** The Jordan plain and the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah lay to the east of Bethel. Literally "toward the east." (Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/13.htm)
- **"They separated themselves":** Literally "a man from his brother." The parting was amicable, by mutual consent, to prevent further strife. (Gill; Pulpit: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-13.html)
- **Guzik:** Lot made his choice purely based on what he could see with his eyes. He cared only for material abundance and was not concerned for the spiritual impact. Abram walked by faith; Lot walked only by sight (2 Corinthians 5:7). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-13/)

### v. 12 — *"Abram lived in the land of Canaan, but Lot settled in the cities of the plain and pitched his tent toward Sodom."*

- **Contrast of lifestyles:** The Pulpit Commentary contrasts the two: Lot desired permanent settlement near wealthy cities; Abram "remained a wanderer throughout its borders, sojourning as in a strange country" (Hebrews 11:9). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-13.html)
- **"Pitched his tent toward Sodom":** Some versions (Pagninus, Montanus, Junius & Tremellius) render this "even unto Sodom." Lot moved progressively closer to the wicked city. (Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/13.htm)
- **Progression of compromise:** Guzik notes that at this point Lot's tent was merely *toward* Sodom. Later (Genesis 19) he sits in the gate as a city leader. Ellicott similarly notes: "Lot sighed for the less self-denying habits of the city" and later "his tent changed to a house." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-13/; Ellicott: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/13.htm)
- **F.B. Meyer:** "Lot walked by sight, choosing the well-watered plains without concern for their spiritual impact… Lot grasped at and lost his all. Abram left and inherited all." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/fbm/genesis-13.html)

### v. 13 — *"But the men of Sodom were wicked, sinning greatly against the LORD."*

- **"Sinners before the LORD exceedingly":** The Pulpit Commentary says this means their wickedness was "restrained neither in quantity nor quality" — it passed all height in arrogance and burst all bounds in prevalence. The phrase "before the LORD" (literally "to Jehovah") is an aggravation: they sinned openly, defiantly, in the very face of God. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-13.html)
- **Did Lot know?** Gill raises the question: either Lot did not know and made his choice ignorantly, or he knew and was tempted by the pleasing prospect of wealth. Jarchi interpreted it: "although they were so, Lot was not restrained from dwelling among them." (Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/13.htm)
- **The Targum of Jonathan** (cited by Gill) lists specific sins of Sodom: defrauding one another, sexual sins, incest, shedding innocent blood, idol worship, and rebelling against the name of the Lord. (Gill)
- **Guzik:** Lot probably thought, "I can serve God as well in Sodom as anywhere else. They probably need a witness there." But he deceived himself (Jeremiah 17:9). It wasn't Lot's choice that led his heart astray — his heart was already astray, and his choice demonstrated it. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-13/)
- **Sermon Bible (J. Ker):** "Lot's choice showed disregard of religious privileges. The sins of the men of Sodom were of a peculiarly gross and inhuman kind; had Lot's religion been warm and bright he would not have ventured among them." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/sermon/genesis/13.htm)

### v. 14 — *"After Lot had departed, the LORD said to Abram, 'Now lift up your eyes from the place where you are, and look to the north and south and east and west,'"*

- **Timing — "after Lot had separated":** God wanted to speak to Abram alone. The promise was only for Abram, not for Lot. (Guzik: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-13/; Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/13.htm)
- **Comfort for loss:** Lot's departure was a grief to Abram — he lost the companionship of the relative who had shared his original abandonment of home, and (being childless) he may have regarded Lot as his heir. God therefore consoles him. (Ellicott: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/13.htm)
- **"Lift up your eyes":** Unlike Lot's self-interested look (v.10), Abram is invited to look at what God has chosen for him. F.B. Meyer: "Lot lifted up his eyes for himself, but when the last of Lot's followers had streamed out of the camp, God bade Abram lift up his eyes, not to choose, but to behold what God had chosen for him." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/fbm/genesis-13.html)
- **The panorama:** From the mountain peaks between Bethel and Ai, one has a commanding view of almost the entire land — north to the hills dividing Judaea from Samaria, south to the Hebron range, east to the mountains of Moab, and west to the Mediterranean. (Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/genesis-13.html)
- **Gill:** God also wanted to assure Abram that though Lot had chosen the most delightful part, it would not be an inheritance to him and his posterity — the whole land would be Abram's and his seed's. (Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/13.htm)

### v. 15 — *"for all the land that you see, I will give to you and your offspring forever."*

- **Renewal of the promise:** This is the third divine revelation to Abram, more specific than previous promises regarding the seed and the land (Genesis 12:2, 12:7). (Constable, via search excerpt)
- **"To you and your offspring forever":** Gill explains that "forever" means until the coming of the Messiah when a new world would begin; it also typifies the heavenly Canaan given to Abram and all his spiritual seed, to be enjoyed forever. Guzik says God repeated the promise to show that Abram's generosity to Lot did not cost him God's provision. (Gill; Guzik: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-13/)
- **Specificity of the promise:** Constable notes three specifics: (1) Abram's heir would be his own seed; (2) God would give the land forever; (3) Abram's descendants would be innumerable. (from search excerpt)

### v. 16 — *"I will make your offspring like the dust of the earth, so that if one could count the dust of the earth, then your offspring could be counted."*

- **Hyperbolic promise:** Gill calls this "an hyperbolical expression denoting the great multitude of Abram's posterity." The impossibility of counting dust underscores the impossibility of numbering Abram's seed. (Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/13.htm)
- **Remarkable for a childless man:** Guzik notes that Abram was in his seventies or eighties and childless. Yet he walked by faith, not by sight. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-13/)
- **"Dust" vs. "stars":** The Pulpit Commentary observes that later the seed is likened to the stars of heaven (Genesis 15:5). Here the "dust" figure connects the seed to the land: "As the land shall be great for thy people, so thy people shall be great for the land" (Lange). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-13.html)
- **Bible.org:** The promise is not to be through Lot — he is gone. Abram believes this promise (cf. Genesis 15:6), and Paul uses this as the basis for justification by grace through faith in Romans 4:3 and Galatians 3:6. (https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-13)

### v. 17 — *"Get up and walk around the land, through its length and breadth, for I will give it to you."*

- **A symbolic act of taking possession:** Constable notes that in the ancient Near East, victorious armies claimed defeated territory by marching through it. By walking the land, Abram is symbolically claiming it by faith. (from search excerpt)
- **Not a literal command:** The Pulpit Commentary says this is "not a literal direction, but an intimation that he might leisurely survey his inheritance with the calm assurance that it was his." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-13.html)
- **Guzik applies it spiritually:** God wants believers to figuratively "walk through" His word — the "land of promise" — possessing its "exceedingly great and precious promises" (2 Peter 1:4) by faith. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-13/)
- **Ellicott:** In the nomad life, repeated change of scene is a necessity — uplands are rich in spring, burnt in summer, exposed in winter. In these journeyings, Abram is to have "the tranquil pleasure of feeling that his seed will inherit each beautiful spot that he visits, and that he is taking possession of it, and hallowing it for them." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/13.htm)

### v. 18 — *"So Abram moved his tent and went to live near the Oaks of Mamre at Hebron, where he built an altar to the LORD."*

- **"Oaks" or "terebinths" of Mamre:** The Hebrew *elon* can mean either oak or terebinth. Mamre was an Amorite chieftain who later became Abram's friend and ally (Genesis 14:13, 24); the grove probably belonged to him. (Pulpit: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-13.html)
- **Hebron:** About 22 miles south of Jerusalem on the way to Beersheba, one of the oldest towns — built seven years before Zoan in Egypt (Numbers 13:22). It is the highest town in the Promised Land at about 3,050 feet elevation. (Pulpit; Constable via search excerpt)
- **The name "Hebron" means "alliance" or "communion":** Ellicott suggests it was so called from the confederacy formed between Abram and the Amorites. (Ellicott: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/13.htm)
- **Spiritual meaning of names:** Guzik notes that Mamre means "vision" and Hebron means "communion" — Abram once again walked in the Lord's vision for him and in communion with the Lord. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-13/)
- **Building another altar:** Abram lived in constant awareness of the need for sacrificial atonement. This is the third altar explicitly mentioned in Abram's journey (Shechem, Bethel, Hebron). (Guzik)
- **El Khalil:** The Pulpit Commentary notes that modern Arabs call Hebron "El Khalil" — "the friend of God," in honour of Abraham. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-13.html)

---

## Points of Comparison Across Traditions

### Abram's Offer to Lot — a Model of Peacemaking vs. a Model of Faith

- **Reformed/Baptist/Evangelical (broad consensus):** All the sources consulted treat Abram's generosity as a model of faith and peacemaking. Matthew Henry: "Those are best prepared for the visits of Divine grace, whose spirits are calm, and not ruffled with passion." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhn/genesis-13.html) The Ligonier devotional (focusing on chapter 14) speaks of Abram as "a man of faith" who "does not allow his nephew's selfishness to become an excuse not to come to his aid." (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/abram-rescues-lot)
- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Guzik/Enduring Word):** Emphasises the spiritual-warfare dimension: conflict arose *after* Abram got right with God because the enemy attacks when believers return to proper worship. Also stresses the "first love" restoration theme with Revelation 2:4-5. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-13/)
- **Older devotional (F.B. Meyer):** Emphasises the contrast between the two men as two types of believers — one spiritual, one carnal. "The world is full of Lots — shallow, impulsive, doomed to be revealed by their choice and end." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/fbm/genesis-13.html)
- **Garner-Howes (Baptist):** Emphasises the covenant aspect — Lot reaped benefits of God's covenant with Abram ("I will bless them that bless thee," Genesis 12:3), and following the departure, Jehovah spoke to reaffirm the land-grant portion of His covenant. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/genesis-13.html)

### "Left" and "Right" — Orientation Debate

- The traditional view (Gill, Pulpit, Ellicott, Constable) is that Abram and Lot stood facing east. "Left" = north, "right" = south. This is the standard Hebrew orientation. (Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/13.htm)
- Constable develops this further: Abram was proposing a partition of the Promised Land, with north (Shechem region) or south (Hebron/Negev) as the two options. (from search excerpt)

### Nature of the Promise in vv. 14-17

- **Dispensational (implied in Constable, Garner-Howes):** The land promise is literal, physical, and eternal — given to Abram's physical descendants. Constable's three specifics emphasise a literal seed and land. (from search excerpt)
- **Covenant/Reformed:** Gill sees the "forever" as extending to the Messianic age, with the land promise typifying the heavenly Canaan. The spiritual seed (Jews and Gentiles in Christ) inherits the promise. (Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/13.htm)
